Identification

1. Machine

This machine is a Johnford DMC-900H vertical machining centre built by Roundtop Machinery Industries in Taiwan, fitted with a FANUC Series 18-MC control.

Machine modelDMC-900H the H denotes No. 50 taper; DMC-900 is No. 40
Machine serialVX1005
Sales orderV159185
BuilderRoundtop Machinery Industries Co. Ltd. — Johnford brand
Original customerAmerican (AMT), USA — customer code 美國AMT
ControlFANUC Series 18-M Model C
Control unit specA02B-0228-B502
Control serialE00905277
Control tested2000-09-20, FANUC Taiwan Ltd.
Machine built2001-02

Current status — September 2026

The SRAM battery failed, the control raised a parity error, and memory was cleared with RESET+DELETE. Parameters, pitch error compensation, PMC parameters and the ATC macro have been restored from the 2001 backup and the machine runs. Tool offsets, work offsets, macro variables and part programs were lost and are being rebuilt.

See Specification and Build sheet.

Before pouring or setting bolts

The foundation sheet prints 650 for one bolt spacing, but the 590 and 50 dimensions it chains with give 640. The foundation bolt sheet (Fig. 9) never lists the DMC-900, so the bolt itself is not specified here: the record carries what is known (M16 × 2.0 J-bolt, M30 × 2.0 adjusting nut, 600 pocket). Measure the machine’s own levelling-screw spacing before committing either.

Every sheet is squared before tracing: the drawing border is located precisely, the photograph’s perspective is removed from its four corners, and the bow of the page along each edge is straightened. It is then traced directly, so all the original detail is kept; the original dimensions are removed and redrawn with DMC-900 values and inches. The side and plan sheets are drawn at DMC-1500 length in the original and are shortened to the DMC-900 as described under each; the transport and lifting sheets are left as drawn.

Levelling and installation

1. Machine

Use a precision level reading 0.02 mm/m per division.

Setup

  • Spindlehead at the centre of Z travel
  • Table centred on the saddle, with the spindle and table centres aligned
  • Saddle centred in Y
  • Traverse the full range of X and Y taking readings

Procedure

  1. Level the machine with the jackscrews around the bed.
  2. Place a test bar on the table with a dial indicator on the spindle, and measure Z movement against X, Y and Z directions.
  3. Trim column inclination with the jackscrews front and rear of the column, to the limits in the Static Accuracy Test Chart.
  4. Check squareness of the spindle centreline to the table with an indicator on a 300 mm sweep.
  5. Adjust so no jackscrew is loose, then secure every jackscrew with its lock nut and tighten the foundation bolts.
  6. Re-check the level.

Foundation bolts are M16 × P2.0 with M30 × P2.0 adjusting nuts, J-type, set 150 mm above the floor before grouting.

Check the level once a month

If it has moved, repeat the adjustment. Lock nuts must be secured even on machines without foundation bolts.

Before first start

  1. Does the power source meet the requirement?
  2. Does air pressure meet the requirement?
  3. Remove all shipping clamps.
  4. Remove rust-proofing with kerosene and a clean cloth.
  5. Clear all obstacles from the machine.

Y was the weakest axis when new

Y sits closest to tolerance on parallelism (0.017 against 0.02) and on squareness to the spindle (0.017 against 0.02), and its positioning error is nearly double X's. That is consistent with the backlash compensation spread — X 0.006, Y 0.041, Z 0.013 — and means the high Y backlash figure is most likely as-built rather than wear. Everything passed with margin; nothing here is a defect. See Servo and backlash.

Power, modes and overrides

2. Operation

Power on and off

Power on

  1. Turn the MAIN POWER SWITCH on the electrical cabinet to I (on). The cabinet fan starts.
  2. Press POWER ON on the control panel to bring up the CNC and display.
  3. Release the EMERGENCY STOP button.
  4. Press NC READY. The hydraulic system starts and the CNC comes ready.
  5. Select ZRN mode and run a manual zero return.

Power off

  1. Confirm the machine is in a safe state.
  2. Stop the spindle.
  3. Press EMERGENCY STOP to stop all drive units.
  4. Press POWER OFF.
  5. Turn the main power switch to O.

Emergency stop effects

Spindle stops; axis movement stops; all driving units stop; the magazine stops if it was changing tools; coolant stops; chip conveyor stops; the door interlock releases once both spindle and coolant have stopped; NOT READY shows on the display.

Zero return

In ZRN mode, CYCLE START runs an automatic reference return. Z returns before X and Y. Individual axes can be homed with the +/− jog buttons. Axis indicators flash during return and hold steady once referenced. Rapid override governs the speed.

If an axis sits close to its reference, move it away first. After power-on or an emergency stop, always run a reference return — there may have been slip on an axis.

Modes

The mode selector feeds X1006.0/.1/.2 (MD1, MD2, MD4). The ladder decodes them into R10.0–R10.7 and drives G43.0–G43.2 to the CNC.

ModeMD4MD2MD1
EDIT000
AUTO001
TAP010
MDI011
HANDLE100
JOG101
RAPID110
ZRN111

This is not the FANUC default decode

On this machine all zeros selects EDIT, not MDI, and MDI is 011. A loss of all three mode signals therefore selects EDIT. Confirmed twice: from the truth table printed on drawing 18M103, and from nets N00003–N00010 of the ladder listing where EDIT is three normally-closed contacts in series.

Diagnosing a stuck mode

  1. SYSTEM → PMC → RUN/STOP — confirm the ladder is running. A stopped ladder drives no G43 at all.
  2. SYSTEM → PMC → PMCDGN → STATUS, display X6, and turn the selector. Bits 0–2 should change. If they do not, it is the switch or its wiring.
  3. If X6 changes but the mode does not, look at R10, then at G43.
  4. Check X8.5 EDKEY — this machine has a separate edit keyswitch input that can block edit mode independently.

Handle

X1 = 0.001 mm, X10 = 0.01 mm, X100 = 0.1 mm per division. Axis selector covers X, Y, Z and 4. The handle works only in HANDLE mode or during handle interruption.

Coolant and air blast

The coolant push button enables M08 and M10; pressed again it disables them, and coolant will not flow even if M08 is executed. Always close the front door before running coolant.

Spindle air blast has its own push button and is also controlled by M07 on, M12 off, and M09 off — the last governed by keep relay K1.7.

Tool display

A two-digit readout driven by Y8.0–Y8.7 (TD11, TD12, TD14, TD18, TD21, TD22, TD24, TD28 — two BCD digits, terminals 104–111). A selector switch at X8.6 MG/STD chooses whether it shows the pocket ready for change or the tool in the spindle.

Overtravel release

  1. Change the mode selector to HANDLE.
  2. Press and hold OVERTRAVEL RELEASE.
  3. Press NC READY.
  4. Use the handle to move the axis back into the working area.
  5. Run a manual reference return on all axes.

Confirm which direction over-travelled before moving. Selecting the wrong direction after release can cause a serious accident. Use a low feed.

Door interlock

Key switch ON makes the interlock effective. OFF allows the door to open with axis movement and spindle rotation unrestricted, but programs can then only be executed in SINGLE BLOCK. Keep relay K1.5 reads "door interlock used".

Software switches

The FANUC software operator's panel — option 9928.5 is enabled. Reach it at OFFSET SETTING → [→] → [OPR], cursor with ↑ ↓, set with ← →.

Recovery notes

1016–1019 follow the use of MACHINE LOCK or Z AXIS LOCK to simulate a program. Recovery is a manual zero return on that axis. Johnford's operation manual references alarm 1015 after MACHINE LOCK and 1018 after Z AXIS LOCK; the ladder holds no message text against 1015.

1013 means the two magazine counters disagree — see Magazine resynchronisation.

P/S 520 is the CNC alarm for a T code outside the valid range.

Alarm 1026 can no longer fire

A6.2, BALANCE PRESSURE ALARM, has no coil anywhere in the loaded ladder. The printed listing raises it at net N00526 straight off X1009.7 DEC8; that net is not in the program the control is running, because the Z-balance logic was reworked into a latch with its own timeout. The message text is still in the table and net N00171 still reads A6.2 as an arm interlock, so the bit still matters — but nothing sets it. Loss of balance pressure will show up as the pump timing out on TB36, not as alarm 1026. Detail in Ladder — how it was recovered.

Pallet changer alarms — not fitted

The ladder carries a complete APC alarm set. No pallet changer is fitted — keep relay K005.3 reads "without auto pallet change" — so these should never appear. They are documented because the I/O they use is shared with the 5th and 6th axis provisions.

If one of these ever does appear, something in the shared I/O has gone wrong rather than a pallet changer having failed. See Axis expansion.

2001 BATTERY POWER LOW is the one that bit this machine

Left unattended it leads to an SRAM parity error and a full memory clear. Change the battery with the control powered on so the SRAM stays alive. See Restore procedure.

Service

4. Maintenance

Service intervals

IntervalTask
DailyCheck lubricating oil level and operation
MonthlyCheck machine level, re-adjust if it has moved
MonthlyZF brake armature clearance, if a braked gearbox is fitted — 0.4 to 1.3 mm, never more
Six monthsCheck guideways and ballscrews for proper lubrication
5000 hoursZF gearbox oil change
Annually or on alarm 2001Replace the SRAM battery — with the control powered on

The battery is the one that costs the most to ignore

A flat battery leads to an SRAM parity error, a full memory clear, and the loss of every tool offset, work offset, macro variable and part program in the control. See What is not backed up.

Lubrication

The centralised lubrication unit sits on the left of the machine and feeds the X, Y and Z sideways and ballscrews through metering valves at the gearbox, saddle and table.

Timing

Factory setting is 5 minutes off, 6 seconds on. On this machine the stored values are T02 = 6250 (exactly 5 minutes) and T01 = 72 (3.46 seconds). See Timers.

Lengthening the off interval too far thins the oil film on the guideways and leads to machine trouble.

Manual lubrication

Press the flat key on the pendant lubricator panel. Use it before start-up, in cold weather, after long disuse, or whenever automatic lubrication seems insufficient.

Alarm conditions

  1. Low oil level — a float switch in the tank
  2. Insufficient pressure — pressure does not rise after the pump runs
  3. Excessive pressure — pressure does not drop after the pump stops
  4. Overload relay trip on the pump

Alarms surface as 1014 LUB. OIL LOW and 2000 LUBRICATION LOW.

Always use the specified grade — another grade will damage the distributors. Check guideways and ballscrews every six months for proper lubrication. Do not supply oil without the filter.

5. Tool Changer

  • Build sheet — 26E01 "#50, CAT, quick change, 24 tools"
  • Keep relays — K004.1 = 0 (16/24/40) and K004.2 = 1 (24/30); the intersection is 24
  • Parts list — 24 boring tool sleeves and 24 CF-12 cam follower bearings

Counters

PMC counters are four bytes each — preset then current. The backup holds:

CounterPresetCurrent
C1366

Check C1 and C2 against 24

Johnford's manual states plainly: "The pocket number of the tool magazine must match the description of C1." This magazine has 24 pockets and the backup holds 36. C1 and C2 agree with each other so alarm 1013 will not fire, but 36 is not 24 — and the control has been restored from this file. Read them at SYSTEM → PMC → PMCPRM → COUNTER with parameter write on, and compare against the physical pocket count before relying on tool search.

Heavy tools

Tools above the standard diameter use T codes T90–T99. The pockets either side must be set to 0 in the tool table and left empty.

Tool change macro O9001

5. Tool Changer

The ATC macro lives in the protected 9000-range program space.

O9001 (ARM TYPE ATC MACRO FOR 16/18)
#100 = #4001
#101 = #4003
#102 = #4120
#103 = BIN[#1032 AND 255]
IF [#102 EQ #103] GOTO1000
G30 G91 Y0. Z0. M6 T#102
N1000 G#100 G#101
M99

It reads the current G-code group modals, compares the commanded tool against the tool currently in the spindle via #4120, and skips the change if they match. Otherwise it sends the machine to second reference and issues the change, then restores the modal state.

This machine's macro differs from the printed manual — correctly

Johnford's manual prints G30 G91 Z0. M6 T#102. This machine has G30 G91 Y0. Z0. M6 T#102. The reason is keep relay K007.2 YZRNTC = 1 — "Y zero return for tool change". The machine is configured to send Y to its reference before a change and the macro matches the configuration. Keep the machine's version. Anyone restoring from the manual instead of the backup would get this wrong.

Program protection

ParameterValueEffect
320200010100Bit 4 (NE9) = 1 — 9000-range programs protected
320310000000
3210 / 3211not setNo program password in use

NE9 being set is why O9001 does not appear in the program directory. Clear bit 4 to see or edit it, and set it back afterwards.

Macro variable dependency

O9001 uses only #100–#103, all volatile and reassigned on every call. Losing the persistent #500 range costs it nothing. What it does depend on is #103 = BIN[#1032 AND 255] — it reads the tool in the spindle from the PMC, so it trusts PMC data that may not match reality after a memory clear.

ATC recovery

5. Tool Changer

Johnford's Section III, sheet 8-1-2. These are the arm-type step codes and their only intended use.

CodeAction
M81Tool arm forward 1 step — returns the arm to its normal position
M83Tool pot down
M84Tool pot up
M86Tool number re-initiate — use with the T.NO/INI switch
M87Unclamp tool on the spindle
M88Clamp tool on the spindle
M77Spindle air blowing
M78Spindle air blowing stop

After an interruption mid-change

A RESET lets the change finish first. An EMERGENCY STOP halts the arm wherever it is. To bring the arm home, M81 returns the tool arm to its normal position.

Single block, and check for interference first

Use these codes in SINGLE BLOCK with a hand on feed hold, and confirm there is no interference before moving the tool, spindle or magazine. Issued out of sequence they will crash the changer. Do not exercise them in MDI to find out what they do — operator message 2008 ARM MAINTENANCE MODE exists for this work.

Magazine resynchronisation

5. Tool Changer

When the pot table no longer matches what is physically in the magazine — after a memory clear, a crash, or a manual tool swap — this is the procedure.

Procedure

  1. OFFSET SETTING → [→] → [OPR]
  2. Cursor to T.NO/INI and set it ON
  3. The CRT shows TOOL NUMBER INITIAL — this is operator message 2006 MAGAZINE INITIAL MODE
  4. In MDI, execute M86 repeatedly to step the tool numbers into agreement with what is physically in each pocket
  5. Set T.NO/INI back OFF

Johnford's wording: "This push button switch is used to turn ON or OFF the tool number initial. This function is using when there was a wrong tool and it was necessary to rearrange the tool numbers… Keep on executing M86 command under the mode of MDI will enable to reorganize the tool number."

Editing the table directly

If the routine will not resolve it, the pot table is directly editable at SYSTEM → PMC → PMCPRM → DATA. Set D21 onward to match what is in each pocket, and correct the counters to the actual carousel position. See Magazine and tool table.

Do the first tool change afterwards in single block with a hand on feed hold.

Tooling interface

5. Tool Changer

Table

Seven T-slots, 18 mm wide on 125 mm pitch, 50 mm from each edge. Section: 18 mm throat, 30 mm base width, 37 mm deep, 12 mm ledge, C4 chamfer.

The pull stud is non-standard — read this before ordering retention knobs

Johnford's drawing is titled "BT-50 Pull Stud — Unstandard Stud For CAT/ISO/DIN 69871 #50 Toolholder". A stock CAT50 or DIN 69871 retention knob is not guaranteed to suit. Measure against this before buying, and keep a known-good sample.

Johnford's own DMC M FUNCTION LIST (16/18), sheet F420056. This is the builder's document and supersedes anything inferred from the ladder.

The slashed descriptions on M80–M86 are handwritten annotations giving the arm-type behaviour alongside the magazine-type wording. This machine is the arm type, so the arm reading applies. See ATC recovery.

How the ladder handles M codes

The decoder

Nets N00177–N00190 are fourteen DECB instructions, each decoding one byte of the M word into eight bits, at decode bases 0, 8, 16 … 104. The outputs land consecutively from R300.0:

DM00 = R300.0   DM08 = R301.0   DM16 = R302.0   …   DM104 = R313.0

giving DM00–DM111. The symbol table names DM00–DM92; the rest are decoded but unnamed. DM46 is misspelt DN46 in the symbol table — a typo in the original source, not a decode artefact.

Every M code's action starts RD R30x.y DMnn, and every M code's completion feeds nets N00480 and N00481, which OR roughly ninety conditions into G5.0 MFIN#1. Those two nets are the machine's entire M-function handshake.

The useful discovery

M71, M72 and M74 write straight into G106, the CNC's mirror image inputs, and M70 clears all three. No option bit, no parameter — they work today.

M24 chip conveyor runs intermittently

N00221  RD DM24 | OR M24R | AND.NOT DM25 | AND ESP.M     -> R104.0 M24R
N00222  RD M24R | OR ?    | AND.NOT T12  | TMR 11        -> R51.2  T11   [CONVEYOR ON]
N00223  RD T11                           | TMR 12        -> R51.3  T12   [CONVEYOR OFF]
N00224  RD M24R | OR ? | (NOT T11 OR K6.0 CHIPTM)        -> Y4.5   CHIP

M24 latches M24R until M25, and the latch drops on emergency stop. T11 and T12 then free-run as an oscillator, and in N00224 the output is gated by NOT T11 OR CHIPTM:

  • K6.0 CHIPTM = 0 — this machine — the conveyor runs only while T11 has not timed out, so it cycles on and off on the T11/T12 periods for as long as M24 is latched.
  • K6.0 = 1 would force the gate true and run it continuously.

A conveyor that appears to stop on its own after M24 is this timer, not a fault. The periods are PMC timers 11 and 12 — readable and settable on the TIMER screen.

M37 drives nothing on this machine

Y3.5 is a dual-purpose output and K7.3 decides which purpose. The symbol table says so outright:

Y1003.5  FLASHER / Z BALANCE          (K7.3 BALANC)

Net N00247 is the selector:

N00247  RD.NOT T9 | OR K6.0 CHIPTM | AND M37R | AND.NOT K7.3 BALANC
        RD.STK R105.1 BALACE | AND K7.3 BALANC
        OR.STK                                         -> Y3.5 FLSHON
  • K7.3 = 0 — Y3.5 is a flasher beacon, driven by M37 and blinked by the T9/T10 oscillator (T9 FLASHER ON, T10 FLASHER OFF).
  • K7.3 = 1 — Y3.5 is the Z-axis counterbalance pump, driven by R105.1 BALACE and nothing else.

K7 = 00001100, so K7.3 = 1

Y3.5 runs the balance pump. M37 still sets M37R and still starts timer T9, but the branch that would reach the output is gated off. M37 and M38 are inert here — they complete in a program and energise nothing. Do not plan an accessory around M37; use a spare Y9 output instead.

Net N00248 shows what actually drives the pump — a pressure-switch latch, interlocked on emergency stop, with no M code at all:

N00248  RD X9.6 DEC7 | RD.STK BALACE | AND.NOT X9.7 DEC8 | OR.STK
        AND ESP.M | AND.NOT TB36                        -> R105.1 BALACE

The symbol table comment on R105.0 reads M37 COVER CLEAN, matching neither the builder's list ("flasher on") nor the output's own comment ("flasher / Z balance pump"). It is a leftover from another build. Where comments disagree, the coil is the answer.

Options and notes

M20 is repurposed here

The manual assigns M20 to chuck close. This machine's ladder symbol at Y3.6 reads SPARE / ALARM LIGHT, and the electrical drawing names terminal 70 ALARM.LIGHT on relay K10. There is no chuck, so the output was reassigned. The ladder and the drawing are the machine-specific truth; the M function list is the generic product document. The two can legitimately disagree this way.

M09 and air blast

Whether M09 also cancels air blast depends on keep relay K1.7. It reads 0, meaning M09 CAN reset M07 — M09 does turn off the air blast. Air blast is also switchable by panel button, and by M07 on / M12 off.

M39 — parts count

Setting 6700 #0 = 1 and 6710 = 39 makes M39 increment the parts count, with BLOCK DELETE switching on automatically once the required count is reached. #3901 = 0 resets it. Alternatively 6080 = 39 makes M39 call macro O9020. Not enabled on this machine.

Macro call

6071 = 6, so M06 calls macro O9001. Parameters 6072 to 6079 are all zero — M06 is the only M code calling a macro. Parameters 3411–3420 are zero, so no non-buffered M codes are defined.

M37 and M38 do nothing on this machine

K7.3 = 1 commits Y3.5 to the Z-axis counterbalance pump, and the ladder branch that would let M37 reach that output is gated off. The codes still complete; they energise nothing. The net-by-net proof is in M functions — what the ladder does.

These are the only travel protection

The ladder ties all twelve hardware limit signals *+L1X … *-L6 permanently ON from the always-ON bit, so the CNC is never told an axis is on a limit. There is no overtravel switch feeding the PMC. After a memory clear, 1320 and 1321 are the only travel protection the machine has — read them back and check them against the pitch-error map, which brackets the same travels independently. Detail in Ladder audit.

Servo, backlash and reference

On the Y backlash figure

Y at 0.041 mm is roughly six times X. The factory accuracy record shows Y was the weakest axis when the machine was new across three independent measures, so this is most likely the as-built value rather than wear. It is still the first thing to re-measure if Y gives circularity or finish trouble.

Reference return

No absolute pulse coders — 1815 reads 0 on all three axes, and deceleration limit switches are wired at X9.0 (X), X9.1 (Y) and X9.2 (Z). The machine homes by deceleration switch and grid every power-up, so there is no APZ procedure and alarm 300 does not apply.

Zero return sequences Z first, then X and Y. If an axis sits close to its reference, move it away before homing.

Pitch error compensation

Each axis is mapped on a 17 mm grid. X uses points 0–53 (54 points, 918 mm), Y uses 100–153 (54 points, 918 mm), Z uses 200–245 (46 points, 782 mm). That brackets the travels correctly.

Stored data

113 of the 1024 points are non-zero, spanning N10002 to N10244. Values run from −7 to +4, i.e. ±0.007 mm at magnification 1. The screws were in good condition when this was measured.

This data cannot be regenerated

It is laser-measured ballscrew data from Johnford. Recreating it needs an interferometer and a full remap. Zero compensation raises no alarm — the machine simply runs less accurately and never tells you. Always restore VX1005.PIC.

Serial (digital) spindle — the analog LSI is not fitted, so the drive is on the serial spindle bus. Motor is a FANUC α15 through a ZF two-speed gearbox.

These carry real configured values rather than defaults, which is one of the cross-checks confirming the rigid tapping licence. The mode switch also has a dedicated TAP position.

Operating limits

Spindle load should be kept below 100 %. Do not run 100–150 % for more than 30 minutes. Spindle override range is 50–150 %.

The spindle will not rotate if the clamp jaw is open, if the gearbox shifted incorrectly, or under emergency stop.

ZF gearbox

8. Spindle & Gearbox

The two-speed unit named in the ladder title is a ZF 2K-series two-speed planetary gearbox for AC and DC main spindle drives. The manual covers 2K10, 2K12, 2K15 and 2K20; which one is fitted must be read off the unit's own plate.

Construction

Sun gear, planet gears, ring gear and spider, with a splined sliding sleeve moved axially by a selector unit driven by a 24 V DC selector motor. Shift position 1 is low speed.

OilCLP to DIN 51517 or HLP to DIN 51524, ISO-VG 68

Contact 2Contact 3SwitchGear
−+S21 : 1 direct — high

Identifying the model

Visual, from the selector unit: 2K10 and 2K12 carry the selector motor on top under a black plastic cover; 2K15 and 2K20 have the motor mounted alongside driving a worm shaft. At 25 HP this machine is almost certainly a 2K15 or 2K20.

If a shift fails

  1. Does the selector motor run at all? Remove the cover and watch it during a shift command.
  2. Is the cross-piece still seated on the motor shaft?
  3. Slipping clutch friction torque within spec?
  4. Limit switch setting — over-travel the shift segment 1.5 to 2 mm past the trip point.
  5. Replace the selector unit as a complete assembly.

On a 2K15 or 2K20 the gears can be selected by hand by turning the worm shaft with a screwdriver, which proves the mechanics independently of the electrics.

ZF's own caution

Never change gear without the oscillatory movement at low speed. Satisfactory shifts cannot be guaranteed otherwise.

Gear change logic

8. Spindle & Gearbox

How the ZF unit maps onto this machine's ladder. This is the chain to walk when gear changes misbehave.

The shift sequence

The spindle motor oscillates — roughly ±8° to 10°, about five direction changes per second, commanded by a 30–50 mV speed reference — so the engagement splines can mesh. A shift normally completes in 300–400 ms.

Timer T03 is ZF's 2-second window

ZF specifies that a shift is abandoned if neither limit switch reports within 2 seconds. Timer T03 GEAR CHANGE FORWARD holds 48 raw units, which at the 48 ms resolution of timers 1–8 is 2.30 seconds. Johnford set the PMC timer marginally above ZF's specification. The two documents agree end to end.

There is also a 10-second limit covering about four attempts, after which the spindle motor is switched off, and the selector motor is de-energised 200 ms after the limit switch confirms. Failure surfaces as alarm 1005 HIGH/LOW GEAR ALARM.

Keep relay K004.5 = 0 — "with high/low gear" — declares the gearbox present, as expected.

PMC type

The order lists PMC-RB control (A02B-0222-H031) with the PMC-RB5 function (A02B-0222-J583#4067) and PMC-RA 3000-step (A02B-0228-H979). Option bit 9946.2 (PMC-RC) is 0, so there is no C/Pascal capability, but RB5 is more capable than base PMC-SB and the on-control programmer function may allow ladder editing without FANUC LADDER-III.

Unidentified enabled bits

Eight enabled bits land on rows the tables leave blank: 9924.2, 9925.2, 9928.7, 9933.2, 9944.5, 9945.7, 9946.0 and 9953.7. 9924 is the language block so 9924.2 is probably a language selection. 9953 is not covered by the tables at all, though the Memex manual references 9953.0 and 9953.1 for FS18C memory sizing.

Why this decode is trustworthy

Four independent cross-checks landed: rigid tapping against the populated 5241/5242 parameters, Macro B against the populated 6000-block and 6071, G68 against the configured 5410 default angle, and high speed skip against an entirely zero 6200 block. The tables themselves are a third-party compilation for 16/18/21-M generally, not a FANUC document for the 18-MC, so treat any single unverified row as working information.

Enabling an option

An option bit is usually the smallest part of the job. There are four layers and every option needs some subset.

  1. The licence bit — what you buy
  2. Executive software — the code must exist in FROM. This machine runs BDB1 Ver 0025, Basic + OPTION-A1
  3. Hardware — LSI, SIMM, amplifier, motor
  4. Configuration — NC parameters, ladder, wiring, macros

How common options tier

TierOptions
Essentially bit-onlyHelical interpolation, G50/G51 scaling, G54.1 extra work offsets, additional macro variables
Bit plus real configurationRigid tapping (5200 block, per-gear speeds, spindle loop tuning), tool life management
Bit plus a projectHigh speed skip, 4th or 5th axis

Worth buying, in order

OptionBitWhy
Additional macro variables9937.4Small, pure software, nothing to configure. Unblocks probing macro suites
Tool offset memory B9935.1Gives geometry/wear separation, which every tool-setter macro assumes
G50/G51 scaling9932.1Bit-only; the 5400-series parameters are already populated
High speed skip9936.4Only after conventional skip probing is proven

Two questions to settle before spending

  1. Will FANUC still write options for a 2001 18-C? Quote against serial E00905277.
  2. Does the option need an executive change? That is a far bigger disruption than a parameter entry and can ripple into other options.

What FANUC hands over

For a control this vintage, the parameter values — not a service visit. Options are often multi-bit: a 4th axis touches the 9900 axis count plus controllable-axes expansion plus additional axis control. Configuration afterwards is the builder's job, or yours.

Memory

9. Control

Two documents disagree with the backup, and the disagreement is in your favour.

SourceSays
Original FANUC orderADDITIONAL SRAM 768 KB — A02B-0222-H076
Factory data sheet9921 = 01000001 — bit 0, 640 m
February 2001 backup9921 = 01000100 — bit 2, 160 m

768 KB is exactly the module size Memex lists for the 18-C (A20B-2900-0351). The upgrade may already be installed and simply under-declared.

Settle it at the boot screen

Power on holding the two right-most soft keys, then BOOT SLOT CONFIGURATION shows MAIN F-ROM and SRAM sizes. Thirty seconds, and it decides whether any purchase is needed at all.

The executive ceiling

Memex's note for the FS18C: reaching 2 MB / 5120 metres needs executive BDBA Ver 0001. On BDB1 Ver 00xx — which is what this machine runs — the ceiling is 1280 metres. Memex can supply BDBA if needed. Their introduction separately claims 768 KB / 1920 metres for 18-B and 18-C, which does not reconcile; confirm the real ceiling before ordering.

Option bits for memory

ParameterBackupBitNowMax per Memex
992101000100.0–.4.2 = 1all 0
994300010000.600 ✓
995310000000.000 ✓
995310000000.101

Sub-memory is unused — 9949 and 9950 are both zero.

Do not set these ahead of the hardware

Declaring more SRAM than is physically fitted is what produces the parity alarms Memex devotes a troubleshooting note to.

Board compatibility

The main CPU board is A16B-3200-0210, which is exactly the board Memex lists as applicable for the 18-C. 18-C SIMM options are A20B-2900-0350 (256 KB), -0351 (768 KB) and -0352 (2.25 MB).

Tool pot table

Navigation: SYSTEM → PMC → PMCPRM → DATA.

What the ladder does with C1, C2 and the table

C1 and C2 are two independent proximity counters — X10.4 CNT1 on the rising edge and X10.5 CNT2 on the falling — cross-checked against each other at net N00513, which raises C12NE and alarm 1013 COUNTER1 NOT EQUAL COUNTER2 when they disagree. C2 is also what ROT uses as the magazine’s current position.

The backup holds presets of 36 and currents of 6. The pocket count ROT works to comes from its own parameter — 0x24, 0x30, 0x32, 0x40, read in BCD as 24, 30, 32 and 40 — gated by the magazine-size relay, and this machine takes the 24 branch. The initialisation nets N00619–N00622 corroborate it: each writes the table length in BCD, and the 24T one writes 0x25 = 25, matching the 25-entry DSCH. A preset of 36 on a 24-pocket magazine is therefore worth reading back on the COUNTER screen, and the current value of 6 is a 2001 snapshot that must match where the magazine physically sits.

The symbol table encodes each entry as a 2-byte bit address, a 6-character symbol and a 2-byte pointer into a packed comment table. The area bases were then pinned by matching against nets in the printed ladder listing: G8.4 ESP.N, F72.7 HANDINT, Y1007.3 HANDLE LED, X1006.0 MD1, R10.0 EDIT, R100.2 APOR, and alarm 1005 at A0.5.

Drawing addresses carry a +1000 offset

PMC ladder — diagram

10. PMC

All 699 nets, drawn in the layout of the FAPT LADDER printout directly from the decoded binary. Nets carry the printed Section VI number, with the binary index underneath. The filter matches net numbers, addresses, symbols and instruction names: HGLS finds every net touching the high gear switch, Y4.6 every net driving the 4th axis clamp, TMRB every fixed timer. A full address or symbol is highlighted where it appears.

Reading it

  • -| |- normally open, -|/|- normally closed. Address above, symbol below. Coils sit on the right rail with the signal comment past it.
  • Cross-references, as on the printout: small numbers above a contact are the nets that write that address; numbers after a coil’s comment are the nets that read it. Click one to jump to that net.
  • Dashed boxes are functional instructions: SUB number and name, then parameters. The input labels (ACT, RST, UPDOWN…) sit on their wires. Every box’s input count matches FANUC’s pin table, which cross-checks the decode.
  • X and Y are written without the printout’s 1000 offset: X1005.6 on paper is X5.6 here, as elsewhere in this reference. Dotted-underlined X/Y addresses open the schematic cross-reference.
  • Search N00226 for a printed net, b00226 for a binary index. Two nets are binary only — in the control but not on paper; see how it was recovered.
  • Instruction list shows the same nets in FANUC mnemonic form (RD, AND.STK, WRT…): execution order, stack operations, and the form any ladder edit is entered in.

Ladder audit — what else it showed

10. PMC

With every operand resolved, the program can be searched exhaustively rather than read selectively. This is what a sweep of all 699 nets turned up — what is driven, what never is, and which values in the backup deserve a look at the machine.

There are no hardware overtravel limits into the PMC

Net N00176 is one rung with twelve coils, and its only condition is the always-ON bit:

N00176  RD R9091.1 LOG1
        WRT G114.0 *+L1X   WRT G114.1 *+L2Y   WRT G114.2 *+L3Z
        WRT G114.3 *+L4A   WRT G114.4 *+5L    WRT G114.5 *+6L
        WRT G116.0 *-L1X   WRT G116.1 *-L2Y   WRT G116.2 *-L3Z
        WRT G116.3 *-L4A   WRT G116.4 *-5L    WRT G116.5 *-6L

These are active-low signals, so tying all twelve high means the CNC is permanently told no axis is on a limit. There is no overtravel switch feeding the PMC on this machine — which is why alarm 1000 OVER TRAVEL has no coil anywhere in the program, and why the limit-switch input block at X13.4–X15.3 is named in the symbol table but never read.

Travel is protected by the stored stroke limit alone — parameters 1320 and 1321. After a memory clear those are the only thing standing between the axes and the ends of the ways, so they are worth reading back and sanity-checking against the pitch-error map, which independently brackets the same travels. Whether a hardwired limit chain exists outside the PMC is a drawing question — ring it out before assuming either way.

Alarms with a message but no coil

Five bits in the A area have text in the message table and nothing that sets them:

BitAlarmTextWhy
A0.01000OVER TRAVELno PMC limit inputs — see above
A0.31003Spindle un/clamp alarm (high/low)variant build
A1.71015X / Y axis machine lockvariant build
A6.21026Balance pressure alarmremoved in the rework — see below
A10.71207APC not readyno pallet changer fitted

All five are still OR'd into the alarm-summary relays, so they behave correctly if anything ever were to set them. Nothing does. Every other bit in the message table has a driver.

The Z-balance interlock is dead, not just the alarm

A6.2 is not only a message — it is a term in the Z-axis interlock:

N00171  ... AND.NOT A0.5 (gear alarm) | AND Y3.4 ZBRK | AND.NOT A6.2 (1026)
                                                    -> G130.2 *IT3Z

In the printed edition, loss of balance pressure raised 1026 and interlocked Z. In the program the control is running, nothing sets A6.2, so that term is permanently true and Z is no longer interlocked on balance pressure. The Z brake term (Y3.4 ZBRK) still applies.

Answered: there is no hardwired backup — both switches go straight into the I/O module and appear nowhere in the emergency-stop chain. See Balance circuit and Y3.5. What replaced the alarm is a pump control loop with none: X9.6 DEC7 (pressure low) starts the pump, it self-holds until X9.7 DEC8 (pressure high) drops it, and TB36 — a 10 second off-delay — is the backstop. TB36 drives nothing else. Worth confirming at the machine whether the balance pressure switch also has a hardwired path; the drawings will say.

The deceleration limit switches — correction

Read by the CNC, not by the ladder

An earlier pass concluded these switches were unused because no net reads them. That was the wrong test. On a Series 16/18 with the built-in I/O card, byte X1009 is the fixed address for *DEC1–*DEC8 and the CNC reads it directly, exactly as it reads X1004.7 SKIP and X1008.4 *ESP without ladder help. So X9.0–X9.2 are the live dog switches for X, Y and Z, reference return is a normal dogged return, and 1425 = 400 is simply the FL speed for it. X9.3 would be *DEC4 for a 4th axis and X9.4 *DEC5. The ladder’s use of X9.6 / X9.7 for the balance circuit is safe only because no 7th or 8th axis will ever exist here.

What the earlier pass said

X9.0 DECX through X9.4 DEC5 are named and presumably wired, and no net reads any of them. The ladder also drives no deceleration signal to the CNC. Only X9.5 DROPLS, X9.6 and X9.7 — the last two repurposed for balance pressure — are live on that byte.

That matters because the encoders are incremental: parameter 1815 is zero on all three axes, so there is no absolute position and reference return happens at every power-on. Parameter 1425 (FL speed) is set to 400, which is a dogged-return setting. How the machine actually decelerates onto the grid is the one thing here best answered by watching it do a reference return.

Values in the backup worth checking

WhatIn the backupWhy it matters
T400 msFAST_ARM UNCLAMP DELAY — on a fast-arm machine this is the only delay between the unclamp confirmation failing and alarm 1004 latching. See below.
C1 / C2 preset36 / 36the magazine has 24 pockets — see Counters and data table
C1 / C2 current6 / 6a 2001 snapshot of where the magazine was; it must match the physical index
T300 msM20/M21 FINISH — harmless, M20 drives a lamp

Every other zero-valued timer belongs to equipment this machine does not have — the pallet changer (T19, T20, T27–T29), the 5th and 6th axes (T31–T36) and the workpiece counters (T13, T14). 28 of the 40 timers are used; none with a value in the file is missing a TMR.

Why T40 stands out

N00494  RD ARMP2 | OR TUCAL | AND M6AR12 | AND.NOT X3.1 TUCLS  -> R191.6 TUCAL
N00495  RD TUCAL | TMR 40                                      -> R54.7  T40
N00496  ... RD.STK T40 | AND K8.7 FASTAM | OR.STK ...          -> A0.4   1004

The alarm latch sets when the arm reaches position 2 during the 1→2 move and the unclamp limit switch has not made. There is no delay in that latch — T40 is the delay, and it is zero. The non-fast-arm branch of N00496 uses TB11 instead, a fixed timer whose value is compiled into the program and therefore survives any memory clear. This machine is K8.7 FASTAM = 1, so it takes the T40 path.

The machine may well have run this way since 2001. But if alarm 1004 ever trips spuriously during a tool change, T40 is the number to raise, and it is settable from the TIMER screen without touching the ladder.

D0–D5 decoded: three PMC spindle-speed commands

The record listed D2–D5 as spindle speed settings that would not decode cleanly as rpm. Nets N00279–N00289 explain them. G32 and G33 are the serial spindle's 12-bit speed command R01I–R12I, and G33.7 is SIND — "take the speed from the PMC, not the program".

N00279/280  normal          MOVE F36 -> G32,  F37 -> G33   (pass the CNC's own command through)
N00281/282/283  OVRIDA      WRT D1.7 ; MOVE D0 -> G32, D1 -> G33
N00284/285/286  GRCH        WRT D3.7 ; MOVE D2 -> G32, D3 -> G33
N00287/288/289  DRINTR      WRT D5.7 ; MOVE D4 -> G32, D5 -> G33

So they are not rpm at all — they are three canned speed commands the PMC substitutes, each with SIND set in bit 7 of the high byte. With parameter 3736 = 4095 as full scale:

ConditionD pairCommandOf full scaleMeaning
OVRIDAD0 / D1 = 0, 000 %spindle stopped
GRCHD2 / D3 = 5, 050.12 %gear-change creep — a few rpm
DRINTRD4 / D5 = 22, −128220.54 %door-interlock limited speed — roughly 32 rpm in high gear

D5 = −128 is 0x80, which is SIND itself, so the stored pair already carries the bit the ladder also sets explicitly. Note that parameter 3735, the minimum speed clamp, is 10 — above the gear-change command of 5, so the creep speed is clamped up to that floor rather than used as written.

Inputs the ladder never reads

AddressSymbolReading
X1.2*1unnamed spare
X4.6ESKIP1high-speed skip — read by the LSI, not the PMC
X4.7SKIP#1high-speed skip — read by the LSI, not the PMC
X9.0–X9.4DECX … DEC5deceleration switches — read directly by the CNC at its fixed X1009 address, not by the ladder (see correction above)
X10.3ATCZRNATC zero-return LS, unused
X13.4–X15.3—a second input block, not fitted

This settles the skip inputs — and a terminal

That the PMC never reads X4.6 or X4.7 is exactly what high-speed skip means: the signal goes to the skip LSI and is timestamped in hardware, bypassing the ladder scan. It confirms the wiring is conventional and that no ladder work is needed to use it — see Probing.

It also resolves the conflict noted in the I/O map: one drawing revision marks terminal 158 SPARE, another calls it HANDLE ENABLE, and the symbol table calls it ESKIP1. Do not count terminal 158 as a free input until it is rung out — if it really is ESKIP1, taking it would cost the skip channel a probe needs.

Two inputs are the other way round — used by the ladder with no symbol at all. The drawings name both: X3.6 is terminal 150, SPINDLE.CO.ALM, and it feeds alarm 1020 SP. LUB/COOLER ALARM at nets 520 and 521. X4.5 is terminal 157, MORI.DN.LS.2H — the magazine orientation-down limit switch, read at nets 330 and 526, raising alarm 1024. Neither is spare.

What the sweep found clean

  • Every named keep relay is used by the program — no dead K bits, and none referenced that the KEEP RELAY screen does not show.
  • Every message-table entry except the five above has a driver, and no bit is driven that lacks a message.
  • Only three Y outputs are never driven — Y0.1, Y1.6 and Y2.0, all magazine functions belonging to other magazine styles. See Spare capacity.
  • No further edition differences. 223 printed net headers were compared against the decode through the offset map; 203 agree outright and the remaining 20 are OCR slips or the printed drawing listing contacts in row order rather than instruction order. Only the Z-balance rework differs. That is 32 % of the printed listing, so it is good evidence against a widespread difference rather than proof of none.

Spare capacity

10. PMC

Correction: Y9 and C77 are not on this board

The .DS reports slot 02 as DI/DO POINTS : 104/72. That is 13 input bytes and 9 output bytes — X0–X12 and Y0–Y8, nothing beyond. The ladder corroborates it exactly: it references every one of X0–X12 and drives every one of Y0–Y8, and touches nothing outside either range.

So Y9 does not exist on this machine, and neither does X18/X19. Terminals 112–119 and 380–391 appear on the drawings because those sheets are generic across VMC550–3000 and cover builds with a larger I/O board. This one stops at X12 and Y8. It also answers the old open item about whether terminals 112–119 are landed in the pendant — there is no byte behind them to land.

Three different things get called "spare" and they are not interchangeable.

What it isWhat this machine has
PMC outputA bit the ladder can driveY9.0–Y9.7 unused
TerminalA screw terminal the point lands on112–119 out; 156/157/158 and 380–391 in
Cabinet relayA physical relay that switches loadK01–K26 all assigned

Spare outputs have no relay behind them

The two output connectors serve different destinations, stated on the drawings:

C74   TO RELAY             Y1000 - Y1004   (ladder Y0 - Y4)
C75   TO OPERATOR'S PANEL  Y1005 - Y1009   (ladder Y5 - Y9)

Every relay-backed output is on C74. The spare byte Y9 sits on C75, which feeds pendant lamps. Terminals 112–119 are lamp-level sourcing outputs from the FANUC I/O module with DOCOM5 as common — there is no relay between them and the load. Fine for a signal into an opto-isolated input; not for switching real current.

Relay-backed outputs whose function is not fitted

OutputRelaySymbolWhy idle
Y0.3—PADECNo pallet changer (K5.3 = 0)
Y3.1—PAF/6CNo APC, no 6th axis
Y3.3—PBD/5CNo APC, no 5th axis
Y4.4K25INDTABNo index table (6710 = 0)
Y4.6K24A4CLNo 4th axis fitted
Y3.2K23APOOnly used with the POWER OFF software switch on

Leave Y4.6 / K24 alone — it is the 4th axis clamp and the machine is otherwise ready for one. Y4.4 / K25 is the least likely to be wanted back, since an index table and a 4th axis are alternatives.

Recommendation

Drive an interposing relay of your own from Y9.0, terminal 112 on C75 with DOCOM5 as common. Mount it on any DIN rail — it does not have to sit on the Johnford interface board. Nothing existing is disturbed, K24 stays available, and seven more points remain on the same connector.

Confirm before wiring

  1. That terminals 112–119 are actually landed in the pendant. The drawing shows the connector pins with the NAME column struck through, which means unassigned — not necessarily unterminated.
  2. The FANUC I/O module's per-point and per-common output rating.
  3. That Y9 is genuinely undriven in the running ladder, by watching it on PMCDGN → STATUS rather than trusting the symbol table alone.

Two build variants on one sheet

C74 is drawn twice, once for VMC and once for DMC. The DMC column matches this machine's ladder — every point checked agrees. The DMC sheet shows Y1.3 as ARM.F2 where this machine's ladder has no symbol, so treat Y1.3 as wired but undriven rather than free.

Correction: 156, 157 and 158 are not three spare inputs

Only one of the three is free. 157 / X4.5 is the magazine orientation-down limit switch — the ladder reads it at nets N00330 and N00526 and raises alarm 1024 from it. 158 / X4.6 is ESKIP1 in the symbol table, SPARE on one drawing revision and HANDLE ENABLE on another. Only 156 / X4.4 has no ladder use. The block to actually use is C77, terminals 380–391 — twelve unassigned points with their own common. See Probe wiring — revised plan.

Balance circuit and Y3.5 — the open question

11. Electrical

Chasing the dead A6.2 interlock through the drawings answered the safety question and opened a better one. The short version: there is no hardwired backup, and what relay K08 actually runs on this machine needs a meter.

There is no hardwired path — the answer to the interlock question

Drawing 18M037 puts both switches straight into the FANUC I/O module with nothing in between:

198  C70-A23  X1009.6  DEC.7  DECELERATION 7   (HYDRAULIC LOW LEVEL)   (DMC3000)
199  C70-B23  X1009.7  DEC.8  DECELERATION 8   (HYDRAULIC HIGHT LEVEL) (DMC3000)

No relay, no contactor coil, no series contact. Searching all 68 drawing sheets: no pressure or level switch appears in the emergency-stop chain, and the electrical part list (18T050) contains exactly one pressure switch in the whole cabinet — item 18, +B5 AIR PRESSURE LOW SWITCH, which is the air circuit and feeds alarm 1002.

So the two switches feed the PMC and nothing else. With A6.2 having no coil in the loaded ladder, nothing anywhere stops the machine on loss of hydraulic balance.

The hydraulic pump runs unswitched

Drawing 18M016 shows the hydraulic pump contactor fed directly from AC110 on wire 6, with no relay contact in the line — unlike every other motor on that sheet, which sits behind a +A2-Kxx contact (K01 coolant, K02 gear-box coolant, K07 M10, K08 chip clean …). The hydraulic power unit therefore runs whenever control power is on. That is the normal arrangement for a Z counterbalance, and it means the ladder's latch is not starting and stopping that motor.

So what does Y3.5 switch?

Three documents name the same output three different ways:

SourceCalls Y1003.5
Drawing 18M101A — the C74 sheet for VPA201A arm type, which is this boardCHIP.CLEAN, relay K08
Same on 18M101C, 18M101G and both the VMC and DMC columns of the C74 listCHIP.CLEAN, relay K08
Ladder symbol tableFLSHON — "FLASHER ON / Z BALANCE PUMP"
Keep relay K7.3's own comment"Y1003.5 FLASHER/Z BALANCE"

The drawings are unanimous and machine-specific; the ladder symbol comments are the generic multi-build names. Johnford's Section VII backs the drawings — it calls timers T9 and T10 the chip-clean on and off timers, and those are exactly the pair that blinks Y3.5 in the K7.3 = 0 branch. The K6.0 CHIPTM term sitting in that same branch — chip conveyor timer control — only makes sense if the output is a chip function.

The testable consequence

This machine has K7.3 = 1, which selects the other branch. So relay K08 is being driven by the hydraulic-level latch instead of by M37 and the chip-clean timers. And because the latch only sets when X9.6 DEC7 makes, if terminals 198 and 199 carry nothing on this machine then Y3.5 never energises at all and K08's load never runs.

The prediction to test: if this machine has a chip washdown and it has never worked, this is why. Three things settle it, none of them difficult:

  1. Put a meter on relay K08 and see what load it feeds — a washdown pump or something in the hydraulic circuit.
  2. Check whether terminals 198 and 199 have switches on them at all, and watch X9.6 and X9.7 on PMCDGN → STATUS.
  3. If K08 is chip clean and 198/199 are empty, K7.3 belongs at 0 — which restores M37 and M38 as well (see M functions).

Do not change K7.3 before checking. If the machine really does have a hydraulic top-up on K08, setting it to 0 takes that away.

One naming note: the drawings call the switches hydraulic low level and hydraulic high level, qualified (DMC3000); the ladder calls them balance pressure low and hydraulic balance high, and alarm 1026 is balance pressure alarm. Level and pressure are different things. Which is on the machine is a look, not a document question.

Schematics — inputs

All 104 inputs the I/O board provides, one sheet per byte, redrawn from the Johnford originals with IEC symbols. Every reference with a dotted underline is clickable — it opens the cross-reference for that component.

How to read these

Left to right: the DC24 rail, the field device, its terminal number, the connector and pin, the PMC address, then the ladder’s own symbol and comment. A point flagged in amber is named but never read by any of the 699 ladder nets. Device symbols are inferred from the name — a limit switch unless the name says otherwise — so treat the symbol as the drawing’s intent, not a guarantee of the part fitted.

Schematics — outputs

11. Electrical

All 72 outputs the board provides. Y0–Y4 go to the VPA201A relay board on C74; Y5–Y8 go to the operator’s panel on C75 and drive lamps.

Two things to watch on these sheets

Amber means never driven — three bits qualify: Y0.1, Y1.6 and Y2.0, all magazine functions belonging to other magazine styles. They are the only spare output bits on the machine.

K18 and K19 each carry a selector between two outputs — K19 between Y0.1 and Y1.6, K18 between Y1.1 and Y2.0. Neither of K19’s sources is driven, so K19 is an idle relay: the one relay-backed spare on the machine.

“No relay on the C74 sheet” means the drawing leaves the K-number column blank for that point. The output exists and the ladder may drive it, but no relay is listed behind it — check before planning to use one. See Probe wiring.

The relay PC board is VPA201A, confirmed on the grounding-system drawing (18M003) which shows VPA002B (+A3) and VPA201A RELAY PC BOARD (+A2).

These K numbers are not PMC keep relays

Same letter, entirely different thing. K01–K26 here are physical control relays in the cabinet. PMC keep relays (K0–K19) are software bits in the control.

Sheet revisions

The VPA201A sheet exists in two revisions: 18M101A, 1999-06-17 with high and low gear on K21/K22, and 18M101C, 2001-09-21 for a Cytec motorised spindle where those positions become spindle cooler, water supply and tool-clean stages. This machine has the ZF gearbox, so the 1999 sheet applies. There is also a VPA101A / VPA301A gear/Geneva type sheet, which is a different magazine drive.

The control side and the power side of the motor circuits together, redrawn from 18M016 and 18M027.

The machine has seven motors on the power distribution sheet: oil hole and coolant, gear box coolant, arm start, magazine, chip conveyor, chip clean, and the hydraulic pump. Each is protected by a Telemecanique GV2-RS motor breaker. On accuracy

The originals are scanned prints with no text layer, so the signal lists were read by OCR and then checked against the ladder — which is exact, having been decoded from the binary. Terminal numbers, addresses, relay numbers and symbols are therefore solid. Device symbols are inferred from names, and the physical arrangement of a cabinet is not represented at all. For anything you are about to put a meter on, the original sheet is the authority.

Backup file set

13. Backup & Restore

The archive VX1005.zip, dated 2001-02-03.

FileContentsNotes
VX1005.DSSystem configuration reportHardware and software slot listing
VX1005.PARFull parameter dump, 2306 linesIncludes 0000–8xxx and 9900–9997
VX1005.PLCPMC ladder, 131 KBMotorola S-record; lives in FROM so it survives a clear
VX1005.PICPitch error compensation, N10000–N11023113 non-zero points
VX1005.DGNPMC parameters — timers, counters, keep relays, data tableRestore data, not diagnostics
VX1005.MRCCustom macro O9001ATC tool change macro

The option parameters survived

Parameters 9900–9998 live in SRAM, so the memory clear wiped them from the control — but they are all in VX1005.PAR. Every licence this machine ever had is in that file. People lose options permanently in exactly this scenario.

File framing

Every file is framed the same way: one 0x12 (DC2) byte, then % … %, then one 0x14 (DC4) byte. Strip the leading DC2 before sending. Memex warns this causes a 930 system alarm on PMC reload. These files carry a single byte, not the dozen the manual anticipates — one character, in a hex-capable editor.

PMC parameter block addressing

BlockContents
N60000–60078Timers
N61000–61078Counters
N62000–62019Keep relays K0–K19
N63000–63022Data table control
N64000–64549Data table D

What is not backed up

The serial backup set covers the control's configuration. It does not cover the working data.

ItemIn VX1005.zip?
NC parametersYes — VX1005.PAR
Option parameters 9900+Yes — in the same file
Pitch error compensationYes — VX1005.PIC
PMC parametersYes — VX1005.DGN
PMC ladderYes — VX1005.PLC (and it lives in FROM anyway)
Macro O9001Yes — VX1005.MRC
Tool offsetsNo
Work offsetsNo
Macro variablesNo
Part programsNo

Close the gap with a PCMCIA SRAM card backup

This is an 18-C, so the card route is available and captures everything in one operation. Power on holding the two right-most soft keys → SYSTEM MONITOR SERVICE MENU → SRAM DATA BACKUP → MAIN. File naming follows the memory size: at 1.0 MB it writes SRAM1_0A.FDB and SRAM1_0B.FDB.

Never initialise the flash from the boot screen — that clears the operating system and the ladder. Initialising the SRAM card itself is fine.

On macro variables

O9001 uses only #100–#103, all volatile, so the ATC macro needs nothing from the persistent #500 range. Any part program that used persistent variables is a different matter.

Restore procedure

13. Backup & Restore

Before anything else

Replace the battery — change it with the control powered on so the SRAM stays alive. Do not move the machine until parameters are back: a cleared control has default servo gains, default stroke limits and no backlash compensation. Confirm the ladder survived at SYSTEM → PMC → LADDER — it lives in FROM and should be intact.

1 — Serial settings

SettingValueSource
Baud96000103 = 11
Data bits7FANUC fixed
ParityEvenFANUC fixed
Stop bits20101.0 = 1
HandshakeDC3 when buffer full0100.5 = 1
Active channel00020 = 0

Cable is a standard FANUC null-modem to DB25 male. 9-pin PC side: Tx 3→3, Rx 2→2, RTS 7→5, CTS 8→4, SG 5→7, frame ground not connected.

2 — Hand-enter these first

You cannot receive the parameter file until the port that receives it is configured.

0000  00000010      0101  10000001
0020  0             0102  0
0100  00101000      0103  11

To write any parameter: OFFSET/SETTING → SETTING → PARAMETER WRITE = 1, then RESET + CAN to clear alarm 100. On the parameter screen you cannot scroll to a number — press the No. key, type it, press INPUT.

3 — Load order

  1. Parameters — VX1005.PAR via SYSTEM → PARAM → OPTR → > → READ → EXEC. Power cycle after.
  2. Verify 9900 = 3 and 9930 = 00001111. If the 9000-range did not write, stop and solve that — every licence rides on it.
  3. Pitch error compensation — VX1005.PIC via SYSTEM → > → PITCH → OPTR → > → READ → EXEC. Do not skip; zero compensation raises no alarm.
  4. PMC parameters — set K17.1 = 1 by hand first, then load VX1005.DGN from the PMC I/O screen: channel 1, device FDCAS, kind PARAM, function READ, EXEC. Some machines need the ladder stopped (SYSTEM → PMC → RUN/STOP → > → STOP) — remember to start it again.
  5. ATC macro — set 3202.4 = 0, load VX1005.MRC via PRGRM → OPTR → > → READ → EXEC, then set 3202.4 back to 1.

4 — Before cutting

  1. Home all three axes. Verify travels and backlash against Servo and backlash.
  2. Resynchronise the magazine before any M06 — see Magazine resynchronisation. The restored pot table is a 2001 snapshot.
  3. Run the spindle through both gear ranges — low to 1090, high to 6000.
  4. Re-touch every tool, rebuild work offsets, reload programs.
  5. Make a PCMCIA SRAM backup.

Reference return

No absolute pulse coders (1815 = 0), so there is no APZ procedure and alarm 300 does not apply. The machine homes by deceleration switch and grid every power-up.

Adding a 4th or 5th axis

14. Projects

The machine-side work for a 4th axis is already done — and a second sweep of the ladder, the parameter file and the drawings shows how it is done, which changes the integration plan in three places: the clamp is automatic, not M-coded; a 4th axis without clamp limit switches will not move until a keep relay is changed; and there is a complete, already-wired handshake for an external index table that needs no licence at all.

The 5th/6th axis I/O is shared with the pallet changer

K5.3 APCVAD = 0 — no pallet changer is fitted, and the slashes in the symbol names are literal: X2.3 TABLE UP LS / +5, Y3.3 PB DEC / 5TH AXIS CLAMP, Y7.6 PA READY LED / 5 REF LED. One ladder covers both build variants, so with no pallets those points are free.

How the 4th-axis clamp actually works — nets N00226–N00231

The M-function list says M27 clamp / M28 unclamp, and 18M023 repeats it. The ladder does something better: M27 and M28 are inert — net N00478 gives them an immediate FIN and nothing else reads them. The clamp is driven from the CNC’s own axis signals instead:

NetDoes
N00226TB26 = 500 ms after axis 4 stops moving (MV4 off) and is in position (INP4 on)
N00227Y4.6 A4CL → K24. With K3.5 4UNCON = 1 (as set) the output is on while the axis is moving or out of position and for 500 ms after, then drops. Output on = unclamp, which is what K24 feeds — the +B2-Y08 A AXIS UNCLAMP solenoid
N00228G126.3 SVF4 servo-off and the Y6.3 lamp = clamped. With K3.4 4THLS = 0 (as set) that is the clamp limit switch X4.0, terminal 152; with K3.4 = 1 it would be timer T25 instead
N00229R104.5 A4UCLR = unclamped, from the unclamp switch X4.1, terminal 153 (or T26). N00172 turns it into the axis interlock G130.3 *IT4A
N00230–231T25 / T26: the timer alternatives, both set to 62

What this means for a rotary with no clamp switches

Most bolt-on rotaries have a brake but no clamp/unclamp confirmation switches. Leave K3.4 = 0 and the axis is permanently interlocked: X4.1 never makes, so *IT4A is never satisfied and A will not move. The fix is a keep relay, not wiring: set K3.4 4THLS = 1 and the ladder confirms clamp and unclamp from T25 / T26 after the output changes. A rotary with no brake at all can still use the same logic with nothing on K24. If the rotary’s brake valve is not 110 V AC, 18M023 provides a spare dry contact A4.NO / A4.COM on the same relay.

The control exposes three axes

The parameter file has axis rows A1–A3 only; 9900 = 3. Parameter 1010 reads 4, which is a remnant of the shared Johnford template — it is clamped to the axis count and does nothing. Both servo axis modules (1/2 and 3/4) are mounted, so the main CPU has a fourth servo channel: 18M008 shows it as JS4A, going to the second port of a two-axis Z/A amplifier. 18M004 shows this machine’s actual build — SV2 is a single-axis Z module with the terminating connector W9 on JX1B — so a 4th axis means a new SVM added to the DC link, W9 moved to it, and a servo cable from JS4A. The licence remains the gate: see below.

The no-licence route: an external index table on M26

18M023 also documents a second, complete circuit that the sweep had not tied together before:

  1. M26 → net N00225 drives Y4.4 INDTAB → relay K25 → dry contact on terminals 262 / 263, labelled FOR INDEX TABLE.
  2. The M-code stays active, and K25 stays closed, until net N00478 sees X4.2 INDEX — the INDEX LS input on terminal 154 — go on. Then FIN, M26 clears, K25 opens.

That is exactly the start / finished handshake a self-controlled indexer uses (Haas HRT with its own control box, Tsudakoma or Yukiwa with a controller, or any pneumatic indexer with a position switch). Pulse count is programmed at the indexer; the CNC only says “go” and waits. No axis licence, no amplifier, no parameters — two wires in and two wires out on terminals that already exist.

Two timing traps

Finished must be a level, not a pulse. N00478 needs X4.2 on at the moment it looks; a short pulse can be missed. And it must be off when M26 starts. If the indexer holds “in position” on continuously, M26 completes instantly, before the index. Most controllers drop the finished output when they see the start contact close; confirm it for the one you buy, or add a relay so 154 sees start-AND-finished.

What has to be bought

ItemNote
Control axes licenceOrder shows A02B-0229-J802#3. Quote J802#4 or J802#5
Controllable axes expansion9943.3 = 0
Additional axis control9927.3 = 0
Servo 5/6 axis moduleOnly for a 5th axis. Used or NOS, roughly $450–1200
Servo amplifierAn SVM1 sized to the new motor for one axis; one SVM2 for two
Motors, rotary or trunnion, cablesThe rotary hardware is usually the largest line

Simultaneous control axes expansion (9943.4) is already on.

Check before committing

  1. Will FANUC still write options for a 2001 18-C? Every other item is commodity hardware with resale value. The licence has no alternative supplier and is the only thing that can kill the project. Quote against serial E00905277.
  2. PSM headroom. A06B-6087-H126 is sized for three servos plus this spindle. Total the continuous draw before adding motors to the DC link.
  3. Rack space and DC link bars. Modules vary in width and the bars are cut to the stack. The terminating connector W9 currently sits on SV2 and would move.

Parameters to set afterwards

1020 axis name (65 = A), 1022 and 1023, 1006 bit 0 for rotary, 1260 degrees per revolution, the 2000-series servo block for the new motor, 1420–1424 feeds, 1851 backlash, and 1320/1321 travel limits. Then set the keep relay and home it.

Five axes controlled is not five-axis simultaneous

3+2 positional is well within reach. Full simultaneous runs into the Series 18 simultaneous-axis ceiling, the absence of tool centre point control on a BDB1-vintage executive, and — probably the real wall — throughput: no DNC1 (9940.0 = 0), no remote buffer (9934.1 = 0), 9600 baud and limited program memory.

Probing

14. Projects

A spindle probe and a tool setter are practical on this machine, but the high speed skip function is not licensed even though the LSI is fitted.

What is present

ItemState
High speed skip LSIMounted on the slot 02 I/O board
High speed skip licence9936.4 = 0 — not licensed
Skip inputX4.7 SKIP, terminal 159
Second skip inputX4.6 ESKIP1, terminal 158
Macro B9933.7 = 1
Skip parameters 6200–6220All zero — never configured
Persistent macro variables#500–#531 only (9937.4 = 0)
Tool offset memoryType A — no geometry/wear split

Conventional skip is enough to start

Plain G31 skip is a base function and X4.7 is already wired. The PMC scan lag is systematic, not random: probe at a fixed touch feed and it folds into the effective probe ball radius when you calibrate, so it cancels. That is why many Renishaw installations run on plain X4.7 and produce good numbers. What HSS buys is freedom to vary feedrate and accuracy at higher touch speeds.

Build the whole setup on conventional skip, prove it, then decide whether the option is worth buying.

Relevant 6200-series bits

From FANUC documentation and field sources, not a manual in hand. Verify against the parameter manual before entering any.

ParamBitNameEffect
62000GSKPMC skip signal also valid for G31
62001SK0Skip polarity — trigger on 1 or on 0
62004HSS0 = conventional skip, 1 = high speed inputs
62005SLSMulti-step skip uses high speed inputs
62006SREEdge — 0 rising, 1 falling
62007SKFDry run / override / accel-decel during G31. Keep 0
62011SEBCompensate accumulated accel-decel pulses
62014IGXDisable conventional skip when HSS is used
6220——Debounce, ×8 ms

Wiring two probes to one input

Series-wire both interface outputs into X4.7. Renishaw solid-state outputs are normally closed, so either one opening triggers the skip, and the two never conflict physically.

Check the radio interface's idle state first

If the RMI output opens when the spindle probe is off, series wiring reads as permanently triggered and the tool setter becomes unusable. This is configurable on most Renishaw interfaces. If it cannot be set the way you need, use a selector relay to route one or the other to X4.7.

Probe start output

A radio probe needs a start signal to its interface. Y9 does not exist on this board (see Probe wiring); the route that survived the drawings sweep is relay K19 on the VPA201A board, fed through its selector from either Y0.1 or Y1.6, both of which the ladder never drives — one added rung and a probe-start M-code gives you a cabinet relay with nothing else on it.

Skip polarity — the parameter that will bite first

6200 is all zeros, so bit 1 SK0 = 0: the control latches position when the skip input goes to 1. Every X input here is 24 V through the device to the terminal, so “1” means a contact closing. A Renishaw interface set to its default normally-closed output opens on touch — the input goes to 0 and G31 never sees it. Either set the interface output to normally-open, or set 6200#1 SK0 = 1 so the control triggers on 0. Series-wiring two probes, as above, relies on the NC convention, so with that scheme SK0 = 1 is the one to use. Verify the bit in the parameter manual before entering it.

Macro B is alive, and two of its settings matter

ParamValueMeaning
60716M06 calls O9001 — the tool change is a macro program, so macro B is installed and running, not just licensed. 6050–6059 (G-code calls) are all 0.
3202#41NE9: the O9000 programs are protected and hidden — expect to lower it to load Inspection Plus, then raise it again.
6001#61CCV: common variables #100–#149 are cleared on reset. Probe results left in #100s do not survive a reset; use #500–#531 for anything that must persist.
6001#71CLV: local variables cleared on reset — normal.

Verifying without moving anything

  1. SYSTEM → PMC → PMCDGN → STATUS, display X4, trigger the probe and watch bit 7. If it does not toggle, it is wiring, not parameters.
  2. Test in air, Z clear: G91 G31 Z-25. F100.
  3. Read the latched position with #5063.

Captured skip positions land in #5061–#5063.

The ladder decode confirms the skip path

The PMC never reads X4.6 ESKIP1 or X4.7 SKIP#1 — searched across all 699 nets. That is exactly what high-speed skip means: the signal goes to the skip LSI and is timestamped in hardware, bypassing the ladder scan. So no ladder work is needed to use it. The flip side is that terminal 158 may not be the spare input the drawing calls it — see Ladder audit before wiring to it.

Wiring

The earlier plan pointed at terminals 156, 157 and 158 as spare inputs. The ladder decode and the drawings between them show that only one of the three is free, and that there is a much better block available.

What changed

TerminalAddressWas calledActually
156X4.4sparefree — no ladder use; but one drawing revision names it MORI.UP.LS, so ring it out
157X4.5sparenot free — it is the magazine orientation-down limit switch, read at nets N00330 and N00526, and it raises alarm 1024
158X4.6sparedo not use — the ladder symbol table calls it ESKIP1, a second skip channel; one drawing says SPARE and another HANDLE ENABLE

Correction: Y9 and C77 are not on this board

The .DS reports slot 02 as DI/DO POINTS : 104/72. That is 13 input bytes and 9 output bytes — X0–X12 and Y0–Y8, nothing beyond. The ladder corroborates it exactly: it references every one of X0–X12 and drives every one of Y0–Y8, and touches nothing outside either range.

So Y9 does not exist on this machine, and neither does X18/X19. Terminals 112–119 and 380–391 appear on the drawings because those sheets are generic across VMC550–3000 and cover builds with a larger I/O board. This one stops at X12 and Y8. It also answers the old open item about whether terminals 112–119 are landed in the pendant — there is no byte behind them to land.

What is actually available

SignalUseWhy
Probe triggerterminal 159 = X1004.7 = SKIP unchanged and confirmed. Named SKIP on two drawing sheets, SKIP#1 in the symbol table, inside the fitted range, and never read by the PMC — the skip LSI timestamps it in hardware.
Spare inputsX4.3 = terminal 155
X4.4 = terminal 156		 the only two bits in X0–X12 that the ladder never reads. 155 is named TOOL.UNPB.2H on one revision and 156 MORI.UP.LS on another, so ring both out — but the addresses are real and free.
Spare outputsY0.1, Y1.6, Y2.0 the only three bits in Y0–Y8 the ladder never drives — MGDEC2, MGDN, MGFOR, all magazine functions belonging to other magazine styles. All three are on C74, the relay side. Whether a relay is populated at those positions needs checking against the C74 sheet.

There is a spare relay after all — K19

The C74 sheet for the VPA201A arm board (18M101A) shows two relays with a selector: K19 is fed from either Y0.1 (MAG.DEC, for the 32-tool magazine) or Y1.6 (ARM.DN, for the air-type arm), and K18 from either Y1.1 or Y2.0.

The ladder drives Y1.1, so K18 is in use. But it drives neither Y0.1 nor Y1.6 — so whichever way K19’s selector is set, K19 sits idle. It is a relay-backed output with nothing driving it.

That makes the probe output a ladder edit rather than a hardware job: drive whichever of Y0.1 or Y1.6 K19’s selector points at, and take the probe-on signal from K19’s contacts. Check the selector on the VPA201A first, and ring out what K19’s contacts are wired to — on an air-arm build they would go to an arm-down valve.

Summary

Two spare inputs (X4.3, X4.4), one idle relay (K19, via Y0.1 or Y1.6), and the skip input (terminal 159) — enough for a probe: trigger on skip, switch on through K19, status on X4.4.

Terminals 156, 157 and 158 — the earlier plan

Of the three the record once called spare, only 156 is free. 157 / X4.5 is the magazine orientation-down limit switch, read at nets N00330 and N00526, raising alarm 1024. 158 / X4.6 is ESKIP1 in the symbol table, SPARE on one drawing revision and HANDLE ENABLE on another — leave it alone either way.

See Probing for the interface and Spare capacity for the output side.

Probing macro suites

Two suites were assessed. The Renishaw one is usable; the Haas one is not worth porting.

Renishaw suite — F-4012-0519-AW

Three things to sort before running it

  1. #120 is set to 9 — a bit field driving three branches. AND 3 = 1 routes to the single-value offset path writing #[2000+#20], which is correct for Tool Offset Memory A. Do not blindly set it to 11 because the header comment says so — that selects the Memory C path writing #12001 and #13001, which do not exist here. The work-offset branch (AND 8) is the unresolved half: bit 3 is currently set, routing to #[2500+#30], where the FANUC 16/18 form would be #[5201+[#30*20]]. Check Renishaw's installation guide.
  2. O9818 is missing — called four times from O9901 with real arguments. O9712/9713/9714 and O9744 are also absent but sit behind disabled branches. Ask Renishaw for O9818.
  3. TWPX/TWPY/TWPZ tokens on three live lines — tilted working plane, which an 18-M will not recognise. They sit behind an unconditional GOTO, but delete them rather than trust that.

The probe start code is already isolated: O9832 has a marked user block defaulting to M50 (PROBE*ON), and O9833 mirrors it for stop. That is where a probe M-code goes.

Haas WIPS v2.8 — not recommended

BlockerDetail

G103178 occurrences in 48 files — lookahead limit, no FANUC equivalent
#6xxxHaas Settings/Parameters access — FANUC has no #6xxx system variables

Size~696 m total, of which the 467 m WIPS/VQC layer is a Haas conversational front end

Porting it is realistically a week of careful work plus proving out, on code that drives a spindle at a stylus. Renishaw's FANUC 16/18 package is the better answer.

How this was extracted

15. Reference

So the work can be repeated or checked.

Parameter and PMC files

.PAR, .PIC, .DGN and .MRC are plain ISO text with a leading DC2 and % framing. They parse directly.

Ladder file

  1. VX1005.PLC is Motorola S-record. Strip the record framing and concatenate the payloads to get 53 864 bytes of PMC image.
  2. The symbol table starts at offset 0x1000, fixed 10-byte records: a 2-byte little-endian bit address, a 6-character space-padded symbol, and a 2-byte pointer into a packed comment table. 977 records.
  3. The comment table is stored character-reversed at the tail of the image. Reverse it and index with each symbol's pointer; comment lengths come from the gap to the next pointer in sorted order.
  4. The PMC message text table is a separate reversed block and can differ in wording from the symbol comments — the message text is what the operator sees.

Address verification

The bit addresses are flat, so the area bases had to be established rather than assumed. They were pinned by matching symbols against nets in the printed ladder listing:

Ladder netSymbolByteBase
G8.4ESP.N8G = 0
F72.7HANDINT584F = 512
Y1007.3HANDLE LED1543Y = 1536
X1006.0MD11606X = 1600
alarm 100510051664A = 1664
R10.0EDIT1700R = 1690
R100.2APOR1790R = 1690
K001.1-XZRN3409K = 3408

The K base was independently cross-checked by value: NOGEAR = 0 agrees with the ladder title's "ZF GEARBOX" and NOATC = 0 agrees with a machine that plainly has a tool changer. The three alternative offsets all give NOGEAR = 1 and contradict both.

Still undecoded

The compiled ladder instruction stream occupies 0x9000 to the end of the PMC image — 17 000 bytes of PMC-SB instructions. Decoding it properly means reverse-engineering the instruction encoding. The printed Section VI listing covers the same ground in readable form.

Ladder — how it was recovered

15. Reference

The ladder in this reference is not a transcription of the printed listing. It was decoded from VX1005.PLC — the control's own compiled program — so it carries no reading or OCR error. Every operand resolves to a named area, and every net carries its number from the printed Section VI listing alongside.

SourceVX1005.PLC
Instruction stream17 000 bytes at offset 0x9000 of the decoded PMC image
Instructions decoded3 755
Undecoded words0
Unresolved operands0
Nets699 (printed listing: 703 — see below)
Ends atSPE, image offset 16258 = printed net N00703

Why not OCR the printed listing

The listing OCRs at roughly 85 % on plain text, but the characters that carry the meaning are the contact symbols — ---||--- against ---|/|---. A single misread there inverts the logic and nothing in the surrounding text would reveal it. Sample output turned ESP.M into ESF.M and G70.7 into 670.7. OCR was used afterwards for one job only — reading the printed net-number column, where a misread is obvious because the numbers must run in order.

Instruction encoding

Basic instructions are four bytes: a two-byte opcode then a two-byte operand, which is a raw bit address.

BytesInstructionBytesInstruction
08 00RD68 00RD.STK
08 02RD.NOT68 02RD.NOT.STK
08 31AND68 31AND.STK
08 33AND.NOT68 33AND.NOT.STK
08 09OR68 09OR.STK
08 0BOR.NOT98 01WRT
40 19OR.STK (stack combine)98 03WRT.NOT
40 21AND.STK (stack combine)98 05 / 98 07SET / RST

Functional instructions begin 00 80 followed by the SUB number, then a fixed-length parameter block. Lengths were measured across every occurrence:

SUB   1:4   2:8   3:6   5:6   6:12   8:12  14:8  15:10  16:10
     17:12 18:12 19:12 20:12 23:8  24:10 25:14 36:14 38:14 40:12
     41:6  59:14 65:10 72:8

Area bases — where the 474 stray operands went

474 operands — one in eight — first decoded to a raw byte address with no area. All of them are now resolved, and the reason turned out to be two separate things.

F and X sit at a different base in the compiled code than in the symbol table. Code F0 is byte 7488 where the symbol table puts it at 512, and code X0 is byte 8128 against 1600. Once that is applied, every one of those 257 operands lands on a standard FANUC F signal — SPL, STL, SA, AL, RST, MF, SF, TF, ZP1–ZP6, MV1–MV6, INP4–INP6 — and not one of them is ever written, which is what F being a CNC-to-PMC area requires. The printed listing shows F34.0 GR10#1 and F34.1 GR20#1 at net N00549, confirming it.

C, D and the system relays were missing from the map. These were settled against VX1005.DGN, the PMC parameter file, whose data-table group definitions are D0–D19, D20–D60 and D500–D549. The ladder's DSCH table head lands exactly on D20, the spindle-tool entry of the magazine table — see Counters and data table.
